tasks.title: Exam-style tasks - 1
tasks.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: For propositions $p,q,r$, the formulas $p\rightarrow(q\rightarrow r)$ and $(p\wedge q)\rightarrow r$ are logically equivalent.
On $D=\{1,2,3,4,5\}$, every $x$ has some $y$ in $D$ such that $x+y=6$.
A museum catalog uses a set $C$ of five distinct codes. Its power set has $31$ members.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Membership checks a listed object, while subset checks every member of the smaller set.

$$R=\{0,\{0\},\{\{0\}\}\}$$

$$\{0\}\in R$$

$$\{0\}\in R\Longrightarrow \{\{0\}\}\subseteq R$$

Both relations are satisfied, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Perform the inner intersection before adding the members of the third set.

$$A\cap B=\{2,4\}$$

$$(A\cap B)\cup C=\{2,4\}\cup\{4,5,8\}$$

$$(A\cap B)\cup C=\{2,4,5,8\}$$

The computed roster matches the claim, so the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Eliminate each implication until both formulas have the same disjunctive form.

$$p\rightarrow(q\rightarrow r)\equiv\neg p\vee(\neg q\vee r)$$

$$(p\wedge q)\rightarrow r\equiv\neg(p\wedge q)\vee r$$

$$\neg(p\wedge q)\vee r\equiv\neg p\vee\neg q\vee r$$

Both formulas reduce to $\neg p\vee\neg q\vee r$, so the statement is True.

**D.** → True

A witness may depend on the universally chosen value of $x$.

$$x\in D$$

$$y=6-x\in\{1,2,3,4,5\}=D$$

$$x+y=x+(6-x)=6$$

The choice $y=6-x$ works for every $x$, so the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Each catalog code may be included or omitted independently.

$$|C|=5$$

$$|\mathcal P(C)|=2^{|C|}$$

$$2^5=32\ne31$$

The power set has $32$ members, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
Topics: 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, 1.4, 1.1.

A: nested membership and subset.
B: intersection followed by union.
C: exporting a conjunction.
D: finite-domain partner.
E: power-set size.

tasks.title: Exam-style tasks - 2
tasks.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: At a conference of $90$ people, $52$ attended the language panel, $41$ attended the data panel, and $18$ attended both. Exactly $17$ attended neither panel.
A rule written $p\rightarrow q$ is always logically equivalent to its converse $q\rightarrow p$.
The sentence $\exists y\in\{1,2,3\}\ \forall x\in\{1,2,3\}\ (x+y=4)$ is true.
Eight delegates form a set $D$. A committee must include Ava and omit Ben and Chen; exactly $32$ committees meet those rules.
For subsets $A$ and $B$ of a fixed universe, $(A\cup B)^c=A^c\cap B^c$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

Inclusion-exclusion counts the union before its complement in the conference.

$$|L\cup D|=|L|+|D|-|L\cap D|$$

$$|L\cup D|=52+41-18=75$$

$$90-75=15\ne17$$

Exactly $15$ people attended neither panel, so the statement is False.

**B.** → False

One truth assignment is enough to disprove a proposed logical equivalence.

$$(p,q)=(F,T)$$

$$p\rightarrow q=F\rightarrow T=T$$

$$q\rightarrow p=T\rightarrow F=F$$

The original implication and its converse disagree, so the statement is False.

**C.** → False

The existential witness must stay fixed while the universal variable changes.

$$x=1\Longrightarrow y=3$$

$$x=2\Longrightarrow y=2$$

$$3\ne2$$

No single $y$ satisfies both required equations, so the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Fixing required and forbidden delegates leaves a free include-or-omit choice for everyone else.

$$8-1-2=5$$

$$\#\{\text{admissible committees}\}=2^5$$

$$2^5=32$$

Exactly $32$ committees are possible, so the statement is True.

**E.** → True

An element outside a union must be outside each set separately.

$$x\in(A\cup B)^c\Longleftrightarrow x\notin A\cup B$$

$$x\notin A\cup B\Longleftrightarrow(x\notin A)\wedge(x\notin B)$$

$$(x\notin A)\wedge(x\notin B)\Longleftrightarrow x\in A^c\cap B^c$$

Both sides have the same elements, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Topics: 1.2, 1.3, 1.4, 1.1, 1.2.

A: two-panel survey.
B: converse of an implication.
C: one witness for all inputs.
D: required and forbidden members.
E: De Morgan union law.

tasks.title: Exam-style tasks - 3
tasks.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The negation of $p\wedge q$ is logically equivalent to $\neg p\vee\neg q$.
Over the integers, $\forall n\ \exists m\ (m>n)$ is true.
The roster $\{\alpha,\beta,\alpha\}$ contains three elements and equals $\{\beta,\alpha\}$.
Finite sets with $|A|=18$, $|B|=14$, and $|A\cap B|=5$ have a symmetric difference of size $23$.
The formula $((p\rightarrow q)\wedge p)\rightarrow q$ is a tautology.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

A conjunction fails precisely when at least one of its parts fails.

$$\neg(p\wedge q)$$

$$\equiv\neg p\vee\neg q$$

$$\neg(p\wedge q)\leftrightarrow(\neg p\vee\neg q)\equiv T$$

This is the conjunction form of De Morgan's law, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Adding one gives a valid integer witness above any selected integer.

$$n\in\mathbb Z$$

$$m=n+1\in\mathbb Z$$

$$m-n=(n+1)-n=1>0$$

Every integer has a larger integer witness, so the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Repeated roster entries do not create new elements of a set.

$$\{\alpha,\beta,\alpha\}=\{\alpha,\beta\}$$

$$\{\alpha,\beta\}=\{\beta,\alpha\}$$

$$|\{\alpha,\beta,\alpha\}|=2\ne3$$

The equality is correct but the claimed cardinality is not, so the statement is False.

**D.** → False

The intersection is removed once from each set's exclusive part.

$$|A\setminus B|=18-5=13$$

$$|B\setminus A|=14-5=9$$

$$|A\triangle B|=13+9=22\ne23$$

The symmetric difference has size $22$, so the statement is False.

**E.** → True

An implication can fail only when its antecedent is true and its consequent is false.

$$(p\rightarrow q)\wedge p=T\Longrightarrow p=T$$

$$p=T\ \text{and}\ p\rightarrow q=T\Longrightarrow q=T$$

$$((p\rightarrow q)\wedge p)\rightarrow q=T$$

No truth assignment makes the formula false, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Topics: 1.3, 1.4, 1.1, 1.2, 1.3.

A: propositional De Morgan law.
B: integer successor witness.
C: duplicate roster entries.
D: symmetric-difference size.
E: modus ponens as a formula.

tasks.title: Exam-style tasks - 4
tasks.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: There exists an integer $g$ such that every integer $n$ satisfies $n\le g$.
If a set $X$ has three elements, then $\mathcal P(\mathcal P(X))$ has $256$ elements.
A campus has $46$ members in art club, $39$ in debate, and $31$ in music; pairwise overlaps are $17$, $12$, and $10$, while $4$ join all three. Exactly $81$ students join at least one club.
No valuation can make at least one of $p,q$ true while also making both $p$ and $q$ false.
The negation of $\forall x\ \exists y\ R(x,y)$ is $\exists x\ \forall y\ \neg R(x,y)$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

Any proposed greatest integer has a strictly larger successor.

$$g\in\mathbb Z$$

$$n=g+1\in\mathbb Z$$

$$g+1\le g\Longleftrightarrow1\le0$$

The successor $g+1$ defeats every proposed witness, so the statement is False.

**B.** → True

Apply the power-set cardinality rule once at each level.

$$|X|=3$$

$$|\mathcal P(X)|=2^3=8$$

$$|\mathcal P(\mathcal P(X))|=2^8=256$$

The second power set has the claimed size, so the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Three-set inclusion-exclusion removes pairwise double counts and restores the triple overlap.

$$|A\cup D\cup M|=46+39+31-17-12-10+4$$

$$|A\cup D\cup M|=116-39+4$$

$$|A\cup D\cup M|=81$$

The at-least-one count is $81$, so the statement is True.

**D.** → True

The last two conjuncts force values that make the first conjunct false.

$$\neg p\wedge\neg q=T\Longrightarrow(p,q)=(F,F)$$

$$(p,q)=(F,F)\Longrightarrow p\vee q=F$$

$$(p\vee q)\wedge\neg p\wedge\neg q=F$$

The formula is false on every assignment, so the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Move the negation inward by switching each quantifier in order.

$$\neg[\forall x\ \exists y\ R(x,y)]\equiv\exists x\ \neg[\exists y\ R(x,y)]$$

$$\neg[\exists y\ R(x,y)]\equiv\forall y\ \neg R(x,y)$$

$$\neg[\forall x\ \exists y\ R(x,y)]\equiv\exists x\ \forall y\ \neg R(x,y)$$

The displayed sentence is the correct negation, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Topics: 1.4, 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, 1.4.

A: greatest integer.
B: iterated power set.
C: three-club union.
D: contradictory requirements.
E: negating alternating quantifiers.

tasks.title: Exam-style tasks - 5
tasks.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: From a six-symbol alphabet containing $x$ and $y$, there are five two-element subsets that include $x$ but exclude $y$.
A greenhouse has $30$ red plants, $22$ fragrant plants, and $9$ that are both. There are $19$ plants that are red but not fragrant.
Exactly two of the four truth assignments for $p,q$ satisfy $(p\vee q)\wedge\neg(p\wedge q)$.
Every novelist is observant, and no observant person is careless. It follows validly that no novelist is careless.
For $E=\{\emptyset,\{\emptyset\}\}$, the empty set is both an element of $E$ and a subset of $E$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

After fixing $x$, the second symbol must come from the unrestricted symbols.

$$6-2=4$$

$$\binom{4}{1}=4$$

$$4\ne5$$

Only four subsets meet the conditions, so the statement is False.

**B.** → False

The red-only region is obtained by removing the overlap from the red total.

$$R=(R\setminus F)\mathbin{\dot\cup}(R\cap F)$$

$$|R\setminus F|=|R|-|R\cap F|$$

$$|R\setminus F|=30-9=21\ne19$$

There are $21$ red nonfragrant plants, so the statement is False.

**C.** → True

The formula requires at least one true proposition but forbids both from being true.

$$(p,q)=(T,F)\Longrightarrow(p\vee q)\wedge\neg(p\wedge q)=T$$

$$(p,q)=(F,T)\Longrightarrow(p\vee q)\wedge\neg(p\wedge q)=T$$

$$(T,T),(F,F)\Longrightarrow(p\vee q)\wedge\neg(p\wedge q)=F$$

Exactly the two mixed rows satisfy the formula, so the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Following one arbitrary novelist through the two premises forces the negated property.

$$\forall x\,(N(x)\rightarrow O(x))$$

$$\forall x\,(O(x)\rightarrow\neg C(x))$$

$$N(a)\Longrightarrow O(a)\Longrightarrow\neg C(a)$$

The universal conclusion follows, so the statement is True.

**E.** → True

The empty set can be listed as an element and is also a subset of every set.

$$\emptyset\in\{\emptyset,\{\emptyset\}\}$$

$$\forall z\,(z\in\emptyset\Longrightarrow z\in E)$$

$$\emptyset\subseteq E$$

Both uses of the empty set are valid, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Topics: 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, 1.4, 1.1.

A: restricted two-element subsets.
B: one exclusive Venn region.
C: exclusive-or truth count.
D: categorical chain.
E: empty-set roles.

tasks.title: Exam-style tasks - 6
tasks.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The biconditional $p\leftrightarrow q$ is equivalent to $(p\wedge q)\vee(\neg p\wedge\neg q)$.
Every violinist is a musician, and Lee is a musician. Therefore Lee must be a violinist.
Whenever finite sets satisfy $A\subsetneq B\subsetneq C$, $|A|=2$, and $|C|=5$, the middle set must have four elements.
In three overlapping mailing lists, the pairwise intersection sizes are $15$, $13$, and $11$, and the triple intersection has size $5$. Exactly $24$ names occur in exactly two lists.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

List the coded sets, form their union, and then retain the unused universal elements.

$$A=\{3,6,9,12,15\}$$

$$A\cup B=\{1,2,3,4,6,9,12,15\}$$

$$U\setminus(A\cup B)=\{5,7,8,10,11,13,14\}$$

The complement roster is correct, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

A biconditional is true exactly when its two propositions agree.

$$(p,q)=(T,T)\Longrightarrow p\wedge q=T$$

$$(p,q)=(F,F)\Longrightarrow\neg p\wedge\neg q=T$$

$$p\leftrightarrow q\equiv(p\wedge q)\vee(\neg p\wedge\neg q)$$

The right side selects exactly the agreement rows, so the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Membership in the larger class does not force membership in its subclass.

$$\forall x\,(V(x)\rightarrow M(x))$$

$$M(\mathrm{Lee})=T$$

$$V(\mathrm{Lee})=F,\quad M(\mathrm{Lee})=T$$

The last line is a countermodel to the conclusion, so the statement is False.

**D.** → False

Strict inclusion forces bounds on the middle cardinality but does not select one value.

$$|A|<|B|<|C|$$

$$2<|B|<5$$

$$|B|\in\{3,4\}$$

A three-element middle set is also possible, so the statement is False.

**E.** → True

Subtract the triple intersection from each pairwise count before adding the disjoint regions.

$$|A\cap B\text{ only}|=15-5=10$$

$$|A\cap C\text{ only}|=13-5=8,\qquad|B\cap C\text{ only}|=11-5=6$$

$$10+8+6=24$$

The exactly-two total is $24$, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Topics: 1.2, 1.3, 1.4, 1.1, 1.2.

A: complement of a coded union.
B: biconditional agreement form.
C: affirming a class inclusion.
D: strict subset chain.
E: exactly two of three sets.

tasks.title: Exam-style tasks - 7
tasks.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Replacing both propositions in a conditional by their negations, without exchanging their positions, always preserves the conditional's truth value.
Over the real numbers, $\forall x\ \exists y\ (y^2=x)$ holds.
A five-element set has exactly $15$ subsets of even cardinality.
For $A=\{1\}$, $B=\{2\}$, and $C=\{3\}$, the equality $A\cup(B\cap C)=(A\cup B)\cap C$ holds.
The expression $p\vee(q\wedge r)$ is logically equivalent to $(p\vee q)\wedge r$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

Compare the formulas on an assignment where the antecedent holds and the consequent fails.

$$(p,q)=(T,F)$$

$$p\rightarrow q=T\rightarrow F=F$$

$$\neg p\rightarrow\neg q=F\rightarrow T=T$$

The inverse can differ from the original implication, so the statement is False.

**B.** → False

A negative input supplies a counterexample because real squares are nonnegative.

$$x=-1\in\mathbb R$$

$$\forall y\in\mathbb R,\quad y^2\ge0$$

$$y^2=-1\ \text{has no real solution}$$

The universal claim fails at $x=-1$, so the statement is False.

**C.** → False

Even and odd subset sizes split the full power set into equal halves.

$$|\mathcal P(S)|=2^5=32$$

$$\#\{\text{even subsets}\}=\frac{32}{2}$$

$$\frac{32}{2}=16\ne15$$

There are $16$ even-cardinality subsets, so the statement is False.

**D.** → False

Evaluating both sides reveals that the proposed placement of the intersection is not distributive.

$$B\cap C=\emptyset\Longrightarrow A\cup(B\cap C)=\{1\}$$

$$A\cup B=\{1,2\}$$

$$(A\cup B)\cap C=\emptyset\ne\{1\}$$

The two sides are different, so the statement is False.

**E.** → False

A counterexample isolates the missing factor of $pee r$ in the proposed expression.

$$(p,q,r)=(T,F,F)$$

$$p\vee(q\wedge r)=T\vee(F\wedge F)=T$$

$$(p\vee q)\wedge r=(T\vee F)\wedge F=F$$

The formulas are not equivalent, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
Topics: 1.3, 1.4, 1.1, 1.2, 1.3.

A: inverse of an implication.
B: universal real square root.
C: even-cardinality subsets.
D: failed distribution pattern.
E: misplaced distributive factor.

tasks.title: Exam-style tasks - 8
tasks.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: In the integer domain, there is an $x$ satisfying $x+y=y$ for every integer $y$.
Define $A=\{n\in\mathbb Z:n^2=16\}$. Then $|A|=2$ and $\{4\}\in A$.
A survey of $100$ residents can have $70$ in group $A$, $50$ in group $B$, and only $10$ in both groups.
Among the eight assignments for $p,q,r$, exactly one falsifies $p\rightarrow(q\vee r)$.
For arbitrary predicates, $\forall x\,(P(x)\vee Q(x))$ is equivalent to $(\forall x\,P(x))\vee(\forall x\,Q(x))$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The additive identity is one fixed witness that works for every integer input.

$$x=0$$

$$x+y=0+y$$

$$0+y=y\quad\text{for every }y\in\mathbb Z$$

The witness $x=0$ proves the sentence, so the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Solving the defining equation identifies elements before any membership claim is checked.

$$n^2=16\Longleftrightarrow n\in\{-4,4\}$$

$$A=\{-4,4\}$$

$$4\in A\quad\text{but}\quad\{4\}\notin A$$

The singleton $\{4\}$ is not one of the integer elements, so the statement is False.

**C.** → False

A union cannot contain more people than the survey population.

$$|A\cup B|=|A|+|B|-|A\cap B|$$

$$|A\cup B|=70+50-10=110$$

$$110>|U|=100$$

The three reported figures are inconsistent, so the statement is False.

**D.** → True

An implication is false only when its antecedent is true and its consequent is false.

$$p\rightarrow(q\vee r)=F\Longleftrightarrow p=T\ \text{and}\ q\vee r=F$$

$$q\vee r=F\Longleftrightarrow(q,r)=(F,F)$$

$$(p,q,r)=(T,F,F)$$

There is exactly one falsifying assignment, so the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Different domain elements may satisfy different sides of the disjunction.

$$D=\{1,2\},\quad P(x)\Longleftrightarrow x=1,\quad Q(x)\Longleftrightarrow x=2$$

$$\forall x\in D\,(P(x)\vee Q(x))=T$$

$$(\forall x\in D\,P(x))\vee(\forall x\in D\,Q(x))=F\vee F=F$$

The countermodel separates the two formulas, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
Topics: 1.4, 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, 1.4.

A: additive identity witness.
B: set-builder roots.
C: feasibility of survey counts.
D: unique falsifying row.
E: universal quantifier over disjunction.

tasks.title: Exam-style tasks - 9
tasks.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: After excluding both $\emptyset$ and the full set, a four-element set has $14$ subsets left.
For any $A,B\subseteq U$, the complement of $A\setminus B$ is $A^c\cup B$.
The logical negation of $p\rightarrow q$ is $\neg p\wedge q$.
The formula $\exists x\,(P(x)\vee Q(x))$ is equivalent to $(\exists x\,P(x))\vee(\exists x\,Q(x))$.
For a four-element ground set $G$, there are $81$ ordered pairs $(A,B)$ with $A\subseteq B\subseteq G$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The excluded endpoints are two distinct members of the power set.

$$|\mathcal P(S)|=2^4=16$$

$$\#\{\text{nonempty proper subsets}\}=16-2$$

$$16-2=14$$

The remaining subset count is $14$, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Rewrite difference as an intersection before applying De Morgan's law.

$$A\setminus B=A\cap B^c$$

$$(A\setminus B)^c=(A\cap B^c)^c$$

$$(A\cap B^c)^c=A^c\cup(B^c)^c=A^c\cup B$$

The proposed identity follows, so the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Rewrite the implication as a disjunction before applying negation.

$$p\rightarrow q\equiv\neg p\vee q$$

$$\neg(p\rightarrow q)\equiv\neg(\neg p\vee q)$$

$$\neg(\neg p\vee q)\equiv p\wedge\neg q$$

The claimed formula reverses both required truth values, so the statement is False.

**D.** → True

A witness for the disjunction witnesses at least one side, and either side supplies a witness for the disjunction.

$$\exists x\,(P(x)\vee Q(x))\Longrightarrow(\exists x\,P(x))\vee(\exists x\,Q(x))$$

$$\exists x\,P(x)\Longrightarrow\exists x\,(P(x)\vee Q(x))$$

$$\exists x\,Q(x)\Longrightarrow\exists x\,(P(x)\vee Q(x))$$

Both directions of the equivalence hold, so the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Each ground element has three possible locations in a nested ordered pair.

$$g\notin B,\qquad g\in B\setminus A,\qquad g\in A$$

$$\#\{(A,B):A\subseteq B\subseteq G\}=3^{|G|}$$

$$3^4=81$$

The ordered-pair count is $81$, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Topics: 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, 1.4, 1.1.

A: nonempty proper subsets.
B: complement of a difference.
C: negating an implication.
D: existential quantifier over disjunction.
E: nested subset pairs.

tasks.title: Exam-style tasks - 10
tasks.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The complement of $A\triangle B$ consists exactly of elements that belong to both $A$ and $B$ or to neither one.
The contrapositive $\neg q\rightarrow\neg p$ always has the same truth value as $p\rightarrow q$.
Every medic is licensed, and at least one medic exists. Hence at least one licensed person exists.
Take $S=\{r,s\}$. Both $\{r\}\in\mathcal P(S)$ and $r\in\mathcal P(S)$ are true.
At an animal shelter, $28$ animals like dogs, $24$ like cats, and $11$ like both. Exactly $35$ like just one of the two.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Symmetric difference records unequal membership, so its complement records equal membership.

$$A\triangle B=(A\cap B^c)\cup(A^c\cap B)$$

$$x\notin A\triangle B\Longleftrightarrow[x\in A\Longleftrightarrow x\in B]$$

$$(A\triangle B)^c=(A\cap B)\cup(A^c\cap B^c)$$

The description matches the complement, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Implication elimination puts the original and contrapositive into the same disjunction.

$$p\rightarrow q\equiv\neg p\vee q$$

$$\neg q\rightarrow\neg p\equiv\neg(\neg q)\vee\neg p$$

$$q\vee\neg p\equiv\neg p\vee q$$

The two formulas are logically equivalent, so the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Apply the universal implication to the witness supplied by the existential premise.

$$\forall x\,(M(x)\rightarrow L(x))$$

$$\exists x\,M(x)\Longrightarrow M(a)$$

$$M(a)\rightarrow L(a)\Longrightarrow\exists x\,L(x)$$

A licensed witness is forced, so the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Members of a power set are subsets of the original set, not its bare symbols.

$$\{r\}\subseteq S\Longrightarrow\{r\}\in\mathcal P(S)$$

$$r\in S$$

$$r\notin\mathcal P(S)$$

The second membership assertion fails, so the statement is False.

**E.** → False

The just-one total is the sum of the two exclusive regions.

$$|D\setminus C|=28-11=17$$

$$|C\setminus D|=24-11=13$$

$$17+13=30\ne35$$

Exactly $30$ animals are in just one group, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
Topics: 1.2, 1.3, 1.4, 1.1, 1.2.

A: complement of symmetric difference.
B: contrapositive equivalence.
C: existence through implication.
D: power-set membership.
E: exactly one of two groups.

tasks.title: Exam-style tasks - 11
tasks.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Under every valuation, at least one direction between $p$ implies $q$ and $q$ implies $p$ is true.
No reptile is warm-blooded, and every snake is a reptile. Therefore no snake is warm-blooded.
If $K\subseteq L$ and $L\subseteq M$, then every element of $K$ belongs to $M$.
If $A$ and $B$ lie in a $15$-element universe with $|A|=12$ and $|B|=9$, then $A\cap B$ has at least six elements.
The formula $(p\leftrightarrow q)\leftrightarrow(\neg p\leftrightarrow\neg q)$ is a tautology.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Expanding the implications exposes a proposition and its negation inside the disjunction.

$$(p\rightarrow q)\vee(q\rightarrow p)\equiv(\neg p\vee q)\vee(\neg q\vee p)$$

$$\equiv(\neg p\vee p)\vee(q\vee\neg q)$$

$$\equiv T\vee T\equiv T$$

The disjunction is true on every row, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

An arbitrary snake inherits reptile status and then the stated exclusion.

$$\forall x\,(S(x)\rightarrow R(x))$$

$$\forall x\,(R(x)\rightarrow\neg W(x))$$

$$S(a)\Longrightarrow R(a)\Longrightarrow\neg W(a)$$

The conclusion holds for every snake, so the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Follow an arbitrary element through the two given inclusions.

$$x\in K\Longrightarrow x\in L$$

$$x\in L\Longrightarrow x\in M$$

$$x\in K\Longrightarrow x\in M$$

The element test proves $K\subseteq M$, so the statement is True.

**D.** → True

The universe size bounds the union and therefore forces an overlap.

$$|A\cup B|\le15$$

$$|A|+|B|-|A\cap B|\le15$$

$$12+9-|A\cap B|\le15\Longrightarrow|A\cap B|\ge6$$

At least six elements must be shared, so the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Negating both propositions preserves whether their truth values agree.

$$p=q\Longrightarrow\neg p=\neg q$$

$$p\ne q\Longrightarrow\neg p\ne\neg q$$

$$(p\leftrightarrow q)\equiv(\neg p\leftrightarrow\neg q)$$

The outer biconditional is always true, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Topics: 1.3, 1.4, 1.1, 1.2, 1.3.

A: comparable implications.
B: negative categorical deduction.
C: subset transitivity.
D: forced minimum overlap.
E: negating both sides of a biconditional.

tasks.title: Exam-style tasks - 12
tasks.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Some artist is a baker, and every baker is creative. Therefore every artist is creative.
Let $T$ have five elements and let $\mathcal F=\{\{t\}:t\in T\}$. Then $|\mathcal F|=5$ and $\mathcal F\in\mathcal P(\mathcal P(T))$.
Among $140$ patients, set sizes are $80$, $65$, and $50$; pairwise overlaps are $30$, $22$, and $18$, with $9$ in all three. Exactly $11$ patients are in none of the sets.
The conjunction $p\wedge(p\rightarrow q)\wedge\neg q$ is satisfiable.
Over $D=\{1,2,3\}$, the statement $\forall x\,(x=1\vee x>1)$ is false.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

The premises control one artist witness but say nothing about all other artists.

$$A(a)\wedge B(a)$$

$$\forall x\,(B(x)\rightarrow C(x))\Longrightarrow C(a)$$

$$A(b)\wedge\neg B(b)\wedge\neg C(b)$$

The object $b$ gives a countermodel to the universal conclusion, so the statement is False.

**B.** → True

Distinct elements produce distinct singleton subsets, all living inside the first power set.

$$|\mathcal F|=|T|=5$$

$$t\in T\Longrightarrow\{t\}\in\mathcal P(T)$$

$$\mathcal F\subseteq\mathcal P(T)\Longrightarrow\mathcal F\in\mathcal P(\mathcal P(T))$$

Both the size and the iterated membership are correct, so the statement is True.

**C.** → False

First count the three-set union, then subtract it from the patient total.

$$|A\cup B\cup C|=80+65+50-30-22-18+9$$

$$|A\cup B\cup C|=195-70+9=134$$

$$140-134=6\ne11$$

Exactly six patients are in none of the sets, so the statement is False.

**D.** → False

The first two conjuncts force the truth of the proposition denied by the third.

$$p=T$$

$$p=T\ \text{and}\ p\rightarrow q=T\Longrightarrow q=T$$

$$q\wedge\neg q=F$$

No assignment satisfies all three conjuncts, so the statement is False.

**E.** → False

Check the alternatives directly for each member of the small domain.

$$x=1\Longrightarrow x=1$$

$$x=2\Longrightarrow x>1$$

$$x=3\Longrightarrow x>1$$

Every domain element satisfies the disjunction, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
Topics: 1.4, 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, 1.4.

A: existential premise versus universal conclusion.
B: family of singletons.
C: none of three groups.
D: inconsistent implication premises.
E: finite-domain disjunction.

tasks.title: Exam-style tasks - 13
tasks.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Two sets with identical power sets must themselves be equal.
The set identity $A\cap(A\cup B)=A$ holds for every pair of sets.
The formula $(p\vee q)\rightarrow r$ is false on four of the eight assignments for $p,q,r$.
Every pilot is trained, and Dana is trained. These facts validly imply that Dana is a pilot.
The set encoded by $\{1,1,2,2,3,3\}$ has six elements.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Singleton membership in a power set recovers membership in the original set.

$$x\in A\Longleftrightarrow\{x\}\in\mathcal P(A)$$

$$\mathcal P(A)=\mathcal P(B)\Longrightarrow\{x\}\in\mathcal P(A)\Longleftrightarrow\{x\}\in\mathcal P(B)$$

$$x\in A\Longleftrightarrow x\in B$$

The two sets have exactly the same elements, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Membership in $A$ already guarantees membership in the larger union.

$$x\in A\cap(A\cup B)\Longrightarrow x\in A$$

$$x\in A\Longrightarrow x\in A\cup B$$

$$x\in A\Longrightarrow x\in A\cap(A\cup B)$$

The two inclusions establish equality, so the statement is True.

**C.** → False

A false implication fixes the consequent as false while requiring a true antecedent.

$$(p\vee q)\rightarrow r=F\Longleftrightarrow p\vee q=T\ \text{and}\ r=F$$

$$\#\{(p,q):p\vee q=T\}=3$$

$$3\cdot1=3\ne4$$

Exactly three assignments falsify the formula, so the statement is False.

**D.** → False

The premise points from pilots to trained people and does not supply the converse.

$$\forall x\,(P(x)\rightarrow T(x))$$

$$T(\mathrm{Dana})=T$$

$$P(\mathrm{Dana})=F,\quad T(\mathrm{Dana})=T$$

A trained nonpilot is a countermodel, so the statement is False.

**E.** → False

A set records whether an object appears, not how many times it is written.

$$\{1,1,2,2,3,3\}=\{1,2,3\}$$

$$|\{1,2,3\}|=3$$

$$3\ne6$$

The encoded set has only three elements, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
Topics: 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, 1.4, 1.1.

A: recovering a set from its power set.
B: absorption law.
C: counting false implication rows.
D: converse predicate inference.
E: cardinality after deduplication.

tasks.title: Exam-style tasks - 14
tasks.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: A Venn diagram has $12$ objects only in $A$, $9$ only in $B$, $7$ in both, and $4$ in neither. The diagram represents a universe of $33$ objects.
The formula $p\rightarrow(q\wedge r)$ is equivalent to $(p\rightarrow q)\wedge(p\rightarrow r)$.
From $\forall x\,(P(x)\rightarrow Q(x))$ and $\exists x\,P(x)$, one may validly infer $\exists x\,Q(x)$.
Among the subsets of a five-element set, exactly $16$ contain at least three elements.
Let $U=\{a,b,c,d,e,f,g,h\}$, $A=\{a,e\}$, and $B=\{a,b,c,d\}$. Then $A^c\cap B=\{b,c,d\}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

The four displayed Venn regions are disjoint and exhaust the universe.

$$|U|=|A\setminus B|+|B\setminus A|+|A\cap B|+|(A\cup B)^c|$$

$$|U|=12+9+7+4$$

$$|U|=32\ne33$$

The diagram contains $32$ objects, so the statement is False.

**B.** → True

Expand both implications and distribute the shared disjunct.

$$p\rightarrow(q\wedge r)\equiv\neg p\vee(q\wedge r)$$

$$\neg p\vee(q\wedge r)\equiv(\neg p\vee q)\wedge(\neg p\vee r)$$

$$(\neg p\vee q)\wedge(\neg p\vee r)\equiv(p\rightarrow q)\wedge(p\rightarrow r)$$

Both sides have the same logical form, so the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Use the existential witness as the input to the universal rule.

$$\exists x\,P(x)\Longrightarrow P(a)$$

$$\forall x\,(P(x)\rightarrow Q(x))\Longrightarrow P(a)\rightarrow Q(a)$$

$$P(a)\wedge(P(a)\rightarrow Q(a))\Longrightarrow\exists x\,Q(x)$$

The argument preserves the witness, so the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Count the allowable subset sizes with binomial coefficients.

$$\#=\binom{5}{3}+\binom{5}{4}+\binom{5}{5}$$

$$\#=10+5+1$$

$$\#=16$$

Exactly $16$ subsets have size at least three, so the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Remove the elements of $A$ from the universe before intersecting with $B$.

$$A^c=\{b,c,d,f,g,h\}$$

$$A^c\cap B=\{b,c,d,f,g,h\}\cap\{a,b,c,d\}$$

$$A^c\cap B=\{b,c,d\}$$

The resulting roster agrees with the claim, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Topics: 1.2, 1.3, 1.4, 1.1, 1.2.

A: reconstructing a Venn universe.
B: implication into a conjunction.
C: universal rule with a witness.
D: large subsets.
E: complement intersected with a roster.

tasks.title: Exam-style tasks - 15
tasks.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Agreement is transitive: whenever $p$ matches $q$ and $q$ matches $r$, the truth values of $p$ and $r$ also match.
From the facts that someone has property $P$ and someone has property $Q$, it always follows that one person has both properties.
Set $A=\{1,2\}$ and $B=\{\{1,2\}\}$. Since $A\in B$, it also follows that $A\subseteq B$.
An element belongs to $A\triangle B\triangle C$ exactly when it belongs to an odd number of the three sets.
The exclusive-or formula $(p\vee q)\wedge\neg(p\wedge q)$ is equivalent to $\neg(p\leftrightarrow q)$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

If the antecedent holds, all three propositions share one truth value.

$$p\leftrightarrow q=T\Longrightarrow p=q$$

$$q\leftrightarrow r=T\Longrightarrow q=r$$

$$p=q=r\Longrightarrow p\leftrightarrow r=T$$

A true antecedent always forces a true consequent, so the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Separate witnesses for the two predicates need not be one common witness.

$$D=\{1,2\},\quad P(x)\Longleftrightarrow x=1,\quad Q(x)\Longleftrightarrow x=2$$

$$(\exists x\,P(x))\wedge(\exists x\,Q(x))=T\wedge T=T$$

$$\exists x\,(P(x)\wedge Q(x))=F$$

The right side can hold without the left side, so the statement is False.

**C.** → False

Being the single listed object of $B$ does not place the members of $A$ directly into $B$.

$$A=\{1,2\}\in B$$

$$B=\{A\}=\{\{1,2\}\}$$

$$1\notin B\Longrightarrow A\nsubseteq B$$

Membership of $A$ in $B$ does not imply $A\subseteq B$, so the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Each symmetric-difference operation toggles membership once for each containing set.

$$0\text{ containing sets}\Longrightarrow0\text{ toggles}\Longrightarrow x\notin A\triangle B\triangle C$$

$$1\text{ or }3\text{ containing sets}\Longrightarrow\text{odd toggles}\Longrightarrow x\in A\triangle B\triangle C$$

$$2\text{ containing sets}\Longrightarrow\text{even toggles}\Longrightarrow x\notin A\triangle B\triangle C$$

Odd membership is exactly the inclusion rule, so the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Exclusive or selects disagreement rows, which are exactly the rows rejected by a biconditional.

$$(p,q)\in\{(T,F),(F,T)\}\Longrightarrow(p\vee q)\wedge\neg(p\wedge q)=T$$

$$(p,q)\in\{(T,T),(F,F)\}\Longrightarrow p\leftrightarrow q=T$$

$$(p\vee q)\wedge\neg(p\wedge q)\equiv\neg(p\leftrightarrow q)$$

The two formulas select the same rows, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Topics: 1.3, 1.4, 1.1, 1.2, 1.3.

A: transitivity of agreement.
B: existential quantifier over conjunction.
C: element versus subset.
D: three-set symmetric difference.
E: exclusive or versus biconditional.

tasks.title: Exam-style tasks - 16
tasks.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The negation of $\exists x\ \forall y\ R(x,y)$ is $\forall x\ \exists y\ \neg R(x,y)$.
The second iterated power set of the empty set is $\mathcal P(\mathcal P(\emptyset))=\{\emptyset,\{\emptyset\}\}$.
Knowing $|A|=20$, $|B|=18$, $|C|=16$, and pairwise intersections $5$, $6$, and $7$ uniquely determines $|A\cup B\cup C|$ as $42$.
Moving the parentheses in the conditional chain from $p\rightarrow(q\rightarrow r)$ to $(p\rightarrow q)\rightarrow r$ never changes its value.
On $D=\{0,1,2\}$, the sentence $\exists x\ \forall y\ (x\le y)$ is true.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Push the negation through the existential and then through the universal quantifier.

$$\neg[\exists x\ \forall y\ R(x,y)]\equiv\forall x\ \neg[\forall y\ R(x,y)]$$

$$\neg[\forall y\ R(x,y)]\equiv\exists y\ \neg R(x,y)$$

$$\neg[\exists x\ \forall y\ R(x,y)]\equiv\forall x\ \exists y\ \neg R(x,y)$$

The proposed quantifier pattern is correct, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Build the two power sets one level at a time.

$$\mathcal P(\emptyset)=\{\emptyset\}$$

$$\mathcal P(\mathcal P(\emptyset))=\mathcal P(\{\emptyset\})$$

$$\mathcal P(\{\emptyset\})=\{\emptyset,\{\emptyset\}\}$$

The displayed roster is complete, so the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Three-set inclusion-exclusion still contains the unspecified triple overlap.

$$|A\cup B\cup C|=20+18+16-5-6-7+|A\cap B\cap C|$$

$$|A\cup B\cup C|=36+|A\cap B\cap C|$$

$$|A\cap B\cap C|\text{ is not given}$$

The union size is not uniquely determined, so the statement is False.

**D.** → False

An assignment with a false first proposition separates the two association patterns.

$$(p,q,r)=(F,T,F)$$

$$p\rightarrow(q\rightarrow r)=F\rightarrow(T\rightarrow F)=T$$

$$(p\rightarrow q)\rightarrow r=(F\rightarrow T)\rightarrow F=T\rightarrow F=F$$

The association of the implications changes the formula, so the statement is False.

**E.** → True

The least domain element supplies one witness below every possible $y$.

$$x=0\in D$$

$$y\in D\Longrightarrow y\in\{0,1,2\}$$

$$0\le0,\qquad0\le1,\qquad0\le2$$

The witness $x=0$ satisfies the universal condition, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Topics: 1.4, 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, 1.4.

A: negating exists-for-all.
B: power sets of the empty set.
C: missing triple intersection.
D: different implication associations.
E: least-element witness.

tasks.title: Exam-style tasks - 17
tasks.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: For $S=\{a,b,c\}$, the proper subset $S\setminus\{a\}$ contains every proper subset of $S$.
If $A\subsetneq B$, then $A\cup B=B$, $A\cap B=A$, and $B\setminus A$ is nonempty.
The formula $p\vee(q\wedge\neg q)$ is a contradiction.
Inside the ordered domain $D=\{0,1,2\}$, choosing the maximum input never obstructs the demand for a strictly larger domain member.
A fixed two-element subset of a seven-element set has exactly $30$ supersets inside that set.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

One proper subset can contain an element omitted by another candidate.

$$S\setminus\{a\}=\{b,c\}$$

$$\{a,b\}\subsetneq S$$

$$a\in\{a,b\}\quad\text{and}\quad a\notin\{b,c\}$$

The proper subset $\{a,b\}$ is not contained in $S\setminus\{a\}$, so the statement is False.

**B.** → True

Proper inclusion determines both basic operations and guarantees a leftover element.

$$A\subseteq B\Longrightarrow A\cup B=B$$

$$A\subseteq B\Longrightarrow A\cap B=A$$

$$A\ne B\Longrightarrow B\setminus A\ne\emptyset$$

All three consequences follow from $A\subsetneq B$, so the statement is True.

**C.** → False

The contradiction inside the parentheses disappears under disjunction with $p$.

$$q\wedge\neg q\equiv F$$

$$p\vee(q\wedge\neg q)\equiv p\vee F$$

$$p\vee F\equiv p$$

The formula is true whenever $p$ is true, so the statement is False.

**D.** → False

The largest domain element cannot have a larger witness inside the same domain.

$$x=2$$

$$y\in D\Longrightarrow y\le2$$

$$\nexists y\in D\;(2<y)$$

The value $x=2$ is a counterexample, so the statement is False.

**E.** → False

A superset already contains the fixed pair and freely chooses among the remaining elements.

$$7-2=5$$

$$\#\{\text{supersets}\}=2^5$$

$$2^5=32\ne30$$

There are $32$ such supersets, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
Topics: 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, 1.4, 1.1.

A: largest proper subset.
B: operations on nested sets.
C: simplifying an impossible conjunct.
D: maximum-element counterexample.
E: counting supersets.

tasks.title: Exam-style tasks - 18
tasks.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Finite sets satisfy $|A|=27$, $|B|=19$, and $|A\cap B|=8$. The region $A\setminus B$ has $17$ elements.
Exactly three assignments for $p,q,r$ satisfy $(p\wedge q)\vee(p\wedge r)\vee(q\wedge r)$.
Every real number $x$ has exactly two real numbers $y$ satisfying $y^3=x$.
When $|S|=4$, exactly $14$ sets $A$ make the strict chain $\emptyset\subsetneq A\subsetneq S$.
In a $60$-element universe, $|A|=35$, $|B|=28$, and $|A\cap B|=15$. Then $|A^c\cup B|=43$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

The part of $A$ outside $B$ is what remains after the intersection is removed.

$$A=(A\setminus B)\mathbin{\dot\cup}(A\cap B)$$

$$|A\setminus B|=|A|-|A\cap B|$$

$$|A\setminus B|=27-8=19\ne17$$

The region $A\setminus B$ has $19$ elements, so the statement is False.

**B.** → False

The formula is true whenever at least two of the three propositions are true.

$$\#\{\text{exactly two true}\}=\binom{3}{2}=3$$

$$\#\{\text{all three true}\}=\binom{3}{3}=1$$

$$3+1=4\ne3$$

Four assignments satisfy the majority formula, so the statement is False.

**C.** → False

The real cube function is strictly increasing and therefore has one inverse value.

$$y_1<y_2\Longrightarrow y_1^3<y_2^3$$

$$y^3=x\Longrightarrow y=\sqrt[3]{x}$$

$$\#\{y\in\mathbb R:y^3=x\}=1\ne2$$

Each real number has one real cube root, so the statement is False.

**D.** → True

The middle set may be any nonempty proper subset.

$$|\mathcal P(S)|=2^4=16$$

$$A\ne\emptyset\quad\text{and}\quad A\ne S$$

$$16-2=14$$

There are $14$ admissible middle sets, so the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Complement the expression by identifying exactly which elements it omits.

$$(A^c\cup B)^c=A\cap B^c=A\setminus B$$

$$|A\setminus B|=35-15=20$$

$$|A^c\cup B|=60-20=40\ne43$$

The union has $40$ elements, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
Topics: 1.2, 1.3, 1.4, 1.1, 1.2.

A: subtracting an overlap.
B: majority formula truth count.
C: uniqueness of a real cube root.
D: strict chains through one subset.
E: union with a complement.

tasks.title: Exam-style tasks - 19
tasks.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: A truth-table report describes the rows where $p$ and $q$ disagree by $(p\wedge q)\vee(\neg p\wedge\neg q)$. The report is correct.
In the rational-number domain, $\exists x\ (x^2=2)$ is true.
The two-element subsets of $\{a,b,c,d\}$ form a five-member family in which no member contains another.
A poll reports $50$ people in $A$, $45$ in $B$, and $20$ in both. Exactly $50$ respondents belong to one of the groups but not both.
From premises $p\vee q$ and $\neg p\vee r$, the conclusion $q\wedge r$ follows validly.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

The displayed right side describes agreement, while the negation of a biconditional describes disagreement.

$$(p,q)=(T,T)$$

$$\neg(p\leftrightarrow q)=\neg T=F$$

$$(p\wedge q)\vee(\neg p\wedge\neg q)=T\vee F=T$$

The two formulas already disagree on the all-true row, so the statement is False.

**B.** → False

A lowest-terms parity argument rules out a rational witness.

$$x=\frac{a}{b},\quad\gcd(a,b)=1,\quad x^2=2\Longrightarrow a^2=2b^2$$

$$a^2\text{ even}\Longrightarrow a=2k\Longrightarrow b^2=2k^2$$

$$a\text{ even and }b\text{ even}\Longrightarrow\gcd(a,b)\ne1$$

No rational witness can square to $2$, so the statement is False.

**C.** → False

Equal-sized distinct subsets cannot contain one another, but the family size still must be counted correctly.

$$\#\{A\subseteq S:|A|=2\}=\binom{4}{2}$$

$$\binom{4}{2}=6$$

$$6\ne5$$

The antichain property holds but the five-member count does not, so the statement is False.

**D.** → False

Remove the shared respondents from each group before combining the exclusive pieces.

$$|A\setminus B|=50-20=30$$

$$|B\setminus A|=45-20=25$$

$$|A\triangle B|=30+25=55\ne50$$

Exactly $55$ respondents belong to one group only, so the statement is False.

**E.** → False

A countermodel can satisfy both disjunctive premises while making one conclusion conjunct false.

$$(p,q,r)=(T,F,T)$$

$$p\vee q=T,\qquad\neg p\vee r=T$$

$$q\wedge r=F\wedge T=F$$

The premises can be true while the conclusion is false, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
Topics: 1.3, 1.4, 1.1, 1.2, 1.3.

A: negated biconditional.
B: rational square root.
C: uniform subsets as an antichain.
D: exclusive-or poll count.
E: overstated resolution conclusion.

tasks.title: Exam-style tasks - 20
tasks.context: Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Premises $\forall x(A(x)\rightarrow B(x))$, $\forall x(B(x)\rightarrow C(x))$, and $\exists x\,A(x)$ entail $\exists x\,C(x)$.
If $\mathcal A\subseteq\mathcal P(S)$, then every member of $\mathcal A$ is a subset of $S$, and $\bigcup\mathcal A\subseteq S$.
An implication $p\rightarrow q$ is true on exactly two of the four assignments for $p,q$.
On every nonempty domain, $\forall x\ \exists y\ R(x,y)$ entails $\exists y\ \forall x\ R(x,y)$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Carry the witness from the first class through both universal implications.

$$\exists x\,A(x)\Longrightarrow A(a)$$

$$A(a)\rightarrow B(a)$$

$$B(a)\rightarrow C(a)\Longrightarrow\exists x\,C(x)$$

The chained deduction produces a $C$ witness, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Unpack the outer subset relation and then follow elements of the union.

$$A\in\mathcal A\Longrightarrow A\in\mathcal P(S)\Longrightarrow A\subseteq S$$

$$x\in\bigcup\mathcal A\Longrightarrow\exists A\in\mathcal A\;(x\in A)$$

$$x\in A\subseteq S\Longrightarrow x\in S$$

Every element collected by the union lies in $S$, so the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Rearrange the two-set inclusion-exclusion equation to isolate the overlap.

$$|A\cap B|=|A|+|B|-|A\cup B|$$

$$|A\cap B|=42+36-70$$

$$|A\cap B|=8\ne6$$

The intersection has eight elements, so the statement is False.

**D.** → False

Only the true-antecedent and false-consequent row falsifies an implication.

$$p\rightarrow q=F\Longleftrightarrow(p,q)=(T,F)$$

$$\#\{\text{false rows}\}=1$$

$$\#\{\text{true rows}\}=4-1=3\ne2$$

The implication is true on three assignments, so the statement is False.

**E.** → False

A relation can provide a different witness for each input without providing one shared witness.

$$D=\{1,2\},\quad R(x,y)\Longleftrightarrow x=y$$

$$\forall x\in D\ \exists y\in D\;(x=y)=T$$

$$\exists y\in D\ \forall x\in D\;(x=y)=F$$

Equality on a two-element domain is a countermodel, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
Topics: 1.4, 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, 1.4.

A: chained rules with existence.
B: family contained in a power set.
C: recovering an intersection.
D: truth count for implication.
E: swapping dependent witnesses.
